name: Australia
summary: Banks (authorised deposit-taking institutions) are prudentially supervised by APRA and conduct-regulated by ASIC, which jointly run the Financial Accountability Regime. AUSTRAC supervises AML/CTF; reformed rules in force since 31 March 2026 require AML/CTF policies to provide personnel due diligence and initial and ongoing training. The Australian Sanctions Office in DFAT administers sanctions, the OAIC enforces the Privacy Act, AFCA resolves complaints and the ATO receives FATCA/CRS reports. Most other duties are competence-based (licensee duties to train representatives, CPS 234, CPS 230, CPS 520) or come from the ASIC-approved Banking Code.

regulators.name: Australian Prudential Regulation Authority
regulators.role: Prudential regulator of banks: capital, governance, fit and proper, operational risk, information security, and co-regulator of FAR.

regulators.name: Australian Securities and Investments Commission
regulators.role: Conduct and licensing regulator for financial services and credit, including DDO, IDR, the Banking Code approval, FAR and the banking SPF code.

regulators.name: Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre
regulators.role: AML/CTF regulator and financial intelligence unit; administers the AML/CTF Act and Rules and receives SMRs and other reports.

regulators.name: Australian Sanctions Office (Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade)
regulators.role: Sanctions regulator under the Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011 and UN sanctions laws; maintains the Consolidated List and issues permits and guidance.

regulators.name: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
regulators.role: Privacy regulator under the Privacy Act 1988 (APPs and Notifiable Data Breaches scheme).

regulators.name: Australian Financial Complaints Authority
regulators.role: External dispute resolution scheme banks must join; will handle scam complaints under the SPF from 2027.

regulators.name: Australian Taxation Office
regulators.role: Receives FATCA and CRS reports from Australian financial institutions under the Taxation Administration Act 1953.

regulators.name: Australian Human Rights Commission
regulators.role: Enforces the positive duty to prevent sexual harassment under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984.

programs.title: Australia | AML/CTF Act 2006 and AML/CTF Rules 2025 Awareness
audience: All bank employees and contractors in AML/CTF roles
programs.why: Since 31 March 2026 a bank's AML/CTF policies must provide for due diligence on, and training of, staff who perform AML/CTF functions. AUSTRAC expects initial training on joining and ongoing refreshers tailored to each role's money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing exposure, with completion records kept.

references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: As amended by the 2024 reforms, the AML/CTF policies must deal with due diligence on people who perform functions relevant to the entity's AML/CTF obligations (para (d)) and with training them on the ML/TF/PF risks the entity faces and on its obligations under the Act, regulations and Rules (para (e)).

references.provision: Sections 5-8 (personnel due diligence) and 5-9 (providing personnel training)
references.note: Policies must cover initial training on joining and ongoing training during employment or engagement; training must suit the person's function, the ML/TF/PF risks of that function and their responsibilities under the policies, and be readily understandable.

references.title: AML/CTF training
references.note: AUSTRAC expects training to cover the entity's obligations and risks, to be tailored by role, refreshed often enough to keep pace with risk and legal change, and recorded.

references.note: Credit licensees must ensure their representatives are adequately trained and competent to engage in the credit activities authorised by the licence.

references.note: Explains how licensees meet the duty to keep advisers trained and competent; advisers on basic deposit and related non-cash payment products can meet the standard through a course assessed by their licensee.

references.title: RG 105 AFS licensing: Organisational competence
references.note: Guidance on the licensee's organisational competence; it notes the separate duty to keep representatives trained and competent. ASIC expects an updated guide in the first quarter of 2027.

references.title: RG 206 Credit licensing: Competence and training
references.note: Credit licensees must keep representatives adequately trained and competent (NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)); ASIC expects initial and ongoing training built into recruitment and supervision.

programs.title: Australia | Banking Code of Practice (2025) Compliance
programs.why: The ASIC-approved 2025 Banking Code commits subscribing banks to train staff to be competent and to understand the Code. It is an industry code binding through contract, not a statute.

references.title: Banking Code of Practice (2025)
references.note: Industry code binding on subscribing banks; it commits banks to train staff to be competent, to know the Code and to deal with vulnerable customers with care.

references.title: 24-136MR ASIC approves enhanced Banking Code of Practice
references.note: ASIC approval of the 2025 Banking Code of Practice (from 28 February 2025), which broadens financial difficulty, improves accessibility and inclusion, and keeps the diligent and prudent banker standard; ASIC notes the Code binds ABA members through their customer contracts and that ASIC does not enforce it.

programs.title: Australia | Responsible Lending (NCCP Act and RG 209)
audience: Home loan and personal lending staff
programs.why: Credit licensees must make reasonable inquiries and assess that credit is not unsuitable, and must keep representatives trained and competent for the credit activities they perform.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 209 Credit licensing: Responsible lending conduct
references.note: ASIC's view of the inquiries, verification and unsuitability assessment required before credit is provided or increased.

references.title: RG 206 Credit licensing: Competence and training
references.note: Credit licensees must keep representatives adequately trained and competent (NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)); ASIC expects initial and ongoing training built into recruitment and supervision.

programs.title: Australia | Internal Dispute Resolution (RG 271)
programs.why: RG 271 sets enforceable standards on complaint timeframes and on staff authority to resolve complaints. ASIC expects induction and ongoing training for complaint staff and IDR awareness for all staff.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 271 Internal dispute resolution
references.note: Sets enforceable IDR standards and expects staff to have authority to resolve complaints; firms should give complaint staff targeted induction and ongoing training and train all staff on the IDR process.

programs.title: Australia | Design and Distribution Obligations (RG 274)
programs.why: Issuers and distributors must take reasonable steps so products reach their target market and report significant dealings. ASIC says it will consider whether distributors have given distribution staff sufficient training and assessed their skills.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 274 Product design and distribution obligations
references.note: Issuers and distributors must take reasonable steps so products reach the target market; ASIC will consider whether distribution staff have had sufficient training, including on product attributes and target markets.

programs.title: Australia | Vulnerable Customers under the Banking Code
programs.why: The 2025 Banking Code broadens the meaning of vulnerability and commits banks to train staff to treat vulnerable customers with sensitivity, respect and compassion. It is an industry code binding through contract.

references.title: Banking Code of Practice (2025)
references.note: Industry code binding on subscribing banks; it commits banks to train staff to be competent, to know the Code and to deal with vulnerable customers with care.

references.title: 24-136MR ASIC approves enhanced Banking Code of Practice
references.note: ASIC approval of the 2025 Banking Code of Practice (from 28 February 2025), which broadens financial difficulty, improves accessibility and inclusion, and keeps the diligent and prudent banker standard; ASIC notes the Code binds ABA members through their customer contracts and that ASIC does not enforce it.

programs.title: Australia | Privacy Act 1988 and APP 11 Security of Personal Information
programs.why: APP 11 requires reasonable steps to protect personal information. The OAIC names staff training as an expected step and says it should reach new starters, contractors and temporary staff.

references.title: Privacy Act 1988
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: An APP entity must take reasonable steps to protect personal information it holds from misuse, interference, loss and unauthorised access, modification or disclosure; training is not named in the Act.

references.title: Chapter 11: APP 11 Security of personal information
references.note: APP 11 requires reasonable steps to protect personal information; the OAIC lists staff training on privacy and security as an expected organisational step.

references.title: Guide to securing personal information
references.note: OAIC guidance that training should reach new starters, contractors and temporary staff, and that all staff should be able to recognise data breaches.

programs.title: Australia | Debt Collection Conduct (RG 96)
programs.why: The joint ASIC-ACCC guideline sets out acceptable collection conduct under consumer and credit laws. It contains no specific training duty, but collections staff need to know it.

references.title: RG 96 Debt collection guideline: For collectors and creditors
references.note: Joint ASIC-ACCC guidance on acceptable contact, communication and conduct when collecting consumer debts; it suggests creditors and collectors build it into staff training and remain responsible for agents.

programs.title: Australia | Sales Practices and Product Suitability
programs.why: Staff who give advice or arrange financial products or credit must be adequately trained and competent under the licensee duties. DDO obligations add target-market controls on distribution.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 146 Licensing: Training of financial product advisers
references.note: Explains how licensees meet the duty to keep advisers trained and competent; advisers on basic deposit and related non-cash payment products can meet the standard through a course assessed by their licensee.

references.title: RG 206 Credit licensing: Competence and training
references.note: Credit licensees must keep representatives adequately trained and competent (NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)); ASIC expects initial and ongoing training built into recruitment and supervision.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 274 Product design and distribution obligations
references.note: Issuers and distributors must take reasonable steps so products reach the target market; ASIC will consider whether distribution staff have had sufficient training, including on product attributes and target markets.

programs.title: Australia | Information Security Awareness (APRA CPS 234)
programs.why: CPS 234 requires banks to maintain information security capability and controls. APRA's CPG 234 suggests an awareness program for staff, contractors and third parties, tracked and tested at onboarding and periodically.

references.title: Banking: prudential and reporting standards (CPS 234 Information Security)
references.note: Lists CPS 234, in force since 1 July 2019, which requires banks to maintain information security capability commensurate with threats.

references.title: CPG 234 Information Security
references.note: Practice guide to CPS 234 suggesting an information security awareness program for staff, contractors and third parties, tracked and tested at onboarding and periodically.

programs.title: Australia | Phishing and Social Engineering Prevention
programs.why: CPG 234 lists social engineering among recurring awareness topics and suggests reporting phishing test results to the board. This is guidance, not a binding training duty.

references.title: CPG 234 Information Security
references.note: Practice guide to CPS 234 suggesting an information security awareness program for staff, contractors and third parties, tracked and tested at onboarding and periodically.

programs.title: Australia | Notifiable Data Breaches Scheme
programs.why: Eligible data breaches must be assessed and notified to the OAIC and affected individuals. OAIC guidance says all staff should be able to recognise a breach and know how to escalate it.

references.title: Part 1: Data breaches and the Australian Privacy Act
references.note: Explains the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme: eligible breaches must be assessed and notified to affected individuals and the Commissioner.

references.title: Guide to securing personal information
references.note: OAIC guidance that training should reach new starters, contractors and temporary staff, and that all staff should be able to recognise data breaches.

programs.title: Australia | Operational Resilience under APRA CPS 230
programs.why: CPS 230, in force since 1 July 2025 and amended from 1 July 2026, requires banks to manage operational risk and keep critical operations within tolerance. Staff must understand their part in it; no course is prescribed.

references.title: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Requires banks to manage operational risk, maintain critical operations within tolerance through disruptions and manage material service providers; replaced CPS 231 and CPS 232. Amended version in force 1 July 2026.

references.title: Final targeted amendments to CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Limited exemption from contractual requirements for certain non-traditional service providers (e.g. central banks, clearing facilities) from 1 July 2026.

references.title: CPG 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: APRA guidance on implementing CPS 230, including business continuity planning, testing and service provider management.

programs.title: Australia | Enterprise Risk Management under APRA CPS 220
programs.why: CPS 220 requires every bank to run a risk management framework covering all material risks, with a Board-approved risk management strategy, a risk management function and a compliance function staffed by suitably trained and competent people. It sets staffing standards for these roles but prescribes no course.

references.title: CPS 220 Risk Management
references.note: Banks must keep a risk management framework suited to their size and complexity, a Board-approved risk appetite statement, strategy and business plan, independent risk and compliance functions (compliance staffed by appropriately trained and competent persons) and a comprehensive independent review at least every three years.

programs.title: Australia | Operational Risk Management (CPS 230 and APS 115)
programs.why: CPS 230 makes banks identify, assess and control operational risk across the business, and APS 115 sets the capital charge for operational risk. Line managers and risk staff need to understand both; no training is prescribed.

references.title: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Banks must manage operational risk effectively, keep critical operations going through disruption and manage risks from service providers.

references.title: APS 115 Capital Adequacy: Standardised Measurement Approach to Operational Risk
references.note: Sets the prescribed method banks use to calculate minimum capital for operational risk.

programs.title: Australia | Credit Risk Management under APRA APS 220
programs.why: APS 220 requires a credit risk management framework with Board-approved strategy, policies and limits, sound credit assessment and ongoing administration. The Board must make sure senior management has the capability to manage credit risk, and policies must reflect staff capabilities; no course is set.

references.title: APS 220 Credit Risk Management
references.note: Banks must keep a credit risk strategy, policies and procedures covering origination, assessment, approval, administration, problem exposures and provisioning; the Board must ensure senior management has the capability and resources to manage credit risk.

programs.title: Australia | Market Risk and Trading Book Capital (APRA APS 116)
audience: Back office and internal audit for trading
programs.why: APS 116 applies to banks with trading books or foreign exchange or commodity positions. Banks using an internal model must have enough staff skilled in such models across trading, risk, audit and back office, and reviews must be done by appropriately trained and competent people. These are competence standards, not a course.

references.title: APS 116 Capital Adequacy: Market Risk
references.note: Sets capital for market risk using the standard method or an approved internal model; internal-model users need skilled staff in trading, risk control, audit and back office and independent review by trained and competent personnel.

programs.title: Australia | Liquidity Risk Management under APRA APS 210
programs.why: APS 210 requires banks to manage liquidity prudently, meet liquidity and funding requirements, run regular stress tests and keep a contingency funding plan. The independent oversight function must be staffed by people with the skills and authority to challenge treasury; no training is prescribed.

references.title: APS 210 Liquidity
references.note: Banks must manage liquidity risk within a Board-set tolerance, stress test regularly across scenarios and maintain an operationally independent oversight function with skilled staff able to challenge treasury.

programs.title: Australia | Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book (APRA APS 117)
audience: Market and balance sheet risk function
programs.why: The revised APS 117, in force since 1 October 2025, sets requirements for managing and holding capital against IRRBB. Reviews of the IRRBB framework must be carried out by independent, appropriately trained and competent people; there is no course requirement.

references.title: APS 117 Capital Adequacy: Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book
references.note: Sets how banks manage interest rate risk in the banking book and calculate capital for it, including APRA approval for the approach used; framework reviews must be done by independent, trained and competent personnel.

programs.title: Australia | Capital Adequacy and Basel III (APS 110, APS 111, APS 112)
audience: Credit and risk staff assigning risk weights
programs.why: APRA's Basel III capital standards require banks to hold adequate capital, meet rules on what counts as regulatory capital and assign correct risk weights to credit exposures. Staff working on capital and risk weighting need to know the rules; no training is prescribed.

references.title: APS 110 Capital Adequacy
references.note: Banks must hold adequate capital at Level 1 and Level 2, keep capital buffers and run an ICAAP, and must tell or seek approval from APRA on changes to capital.

references.title: APS 111 Capital Adequacy: Measurement of Capital
references.note: Sets the features an instrument needs to count as regulatory capital and the deductions and adjustments to capital.

references.title: APS 112 Capital Adequacy: Standardised Approach to Credit Risk
references.note: Requires policies and processes so that the correct risk weights are given to credit exposures under the standardised approach.

programs.title: Australia | Stress Testing and ICAAP (CPS 220, APS 110, APS 210)
programs.why: Banks must build forward-looking scenario analysis and stress testing on severe but plausible assumptions into risk management, run an ICAAP and stress test liquidity regularly. The people who design and use these tests need the know-how; no course is required.

references.title: CPS 220 Risk Management
references.note: The risk management framework must include forward-looking scenario analysis and stress testing based on severe but plausible assumptions, supported by adequate risk data.

references.title: APS 110 Capital Adequacy
references.note: Banks must have a documented, Board-approved ICAAP, including stress testing and capital planning, with a summary statement covering its required elements.

references.title: APS 210 Liquidity
references.note: Requires regular liquidity stress tests over short and protracted, institution-specific and market-wide scenarios.

programs.title: Australia | Risk Appetite Statement and Risk Culture (CPS 220)
programs.why: Under CPS 220 the Board sets the risk appetite, approves the risk appetite statement and forms a view of risk culture, and management must run the business within that appetite. This expects informed boards and managers but sets no training course.

references.title: CPS 220 Risk Management
references.note: The Board must set risk appetite, approve the risk appetite statement and risk management strategy, and form a view on the bank's risk culture and any changes needed.

programs.title: Australia | Internal Ratings Models and Credit Risk Control (APRA APS 113)
programs.why: APS 113, in a new version from 30 June 2026, applies to banks approved (or seeking approval) to use internal ratings-based models for credit risk capital. Staff of the credit risk control unit must have the knowledge, skills, tools and resources for their role; this is a competence standard, not a course.

references.title: APS 113 Capital Adequacy: Internal Ratings-based Approach to Credit Risk
references.note: Sets requirements for IRB approval and use, including rating systems, estimates and validation; credit risk control unit personnel must have the knowledge and skills to do their job.

programs.title: Australia | Large Exposures and Concentration Risk (APRA APS 221)
programs.why: APS 221 requires banks to set prudent limits and policies to monitor and control large exposures and risk concentrations. Credit and risk staff need to understand how exposures are aggregated and limited; no training is prescribed.

references.title: APS 221 Large Exposures
references.note: Banks must have policies, systems and limits to monitor and control large exposures to counterparties and connected groups and other risk concentrations.

programs.title: Australia | Material Service Provider Management (CPS 230)
programs.why: CPS 230 replaced CPS 231 on outsourcing. Banks must manage material service providers through policy, due diligence, contracts and monitoring, with narrow exemptions for some providers from 1 July 2026.

references.title: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Requires banks to manage operational risk, maintain critical operations within tolerance through disruptions and manage material service providers; replaced CPS 231 and CPS 232. Amended version in force 1 July 2026.

references.title: Final targeted amendments to CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Limited exemption from contractual requirements for certain non-traditional service providers (e.g. central banks, clearing facilities) from 1 July 2026.

programs.title: Australia | Business Continuity under CPS 230
programs.why: CPS 230 replaced CPS 232 and requires a credible business continuity plan with regular testing. Staff involved need to know their roles; no course is prescribed.

references.title: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Requires banks to manage operational risk, maintain critical operations within tolerance through disruptions and manage material service providers; replaced CPS 231 and CPS 232. Amended version in force 1 July 2026.

references.title: CPG 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: APRA guidance on implementing CPS 230, including business continuity planning, testing and service provider management.

programs.title: Australia | Recovery, Exit and Resolution Planning (CPS 190 and CPS 900)
programs.why: CPS 190 makes banks keep a credible recovery and exit plan and the capabilities to carry it out, and CPS 900 requires larger and critical-function banks to support APRA resolution planning. Reviews and resolvability assessments must be done by competent, experienced people; no course is set.

references.title: CPS 190 Recovery and Exit Planning
references.note: Banks must keep a credible recovery and exit plan, maintain the capabilities to execute it and, for significant institutions, have it reviewed by independent, experienced and competent persons at least every three years.

references.title: CPS 900 Resolution Planning
references.note: Significant banks and those with critical functions must build resolution capabilities, run resolvability assessments with suitably skilled personnel and remove barriers to resolution.

programs.title: Australia | Non-performing and Restructured Exposures (APRA APS 220)
programs.why: APS 220 defines non-performing (in default) and restructured exposures and requires early identification and management of problem exposures. Staff who grade loans need to apply these definitions consistently; no training is required by the text.

references.title: APS 220 Credit Risk Management
references.note: Defines non-performing and restructured exposures, including indicators of unlikeliness to pay and past-due treatment, and requires prudent processes to identify and manage problem exposures early.

programs.title: Australia | Hardship Variations and Loan Restructuring (National Credit Code)
programs.why: Borrowers under regulated credit can give a hardship notice orally or in writing, and lenders must respond within set timeframes before enforcing. APS 220 also governs how restructured exposures are treated. Staff must recognise and handle hardship requests correctly; no course is prescribed.

references.title: National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: A debtor may give a hardship notice orally or in writing; the credit provider may request information within 21 days and must deal with the notice, and hardship notices affect enforcement.

references.title: APS 220 Credit Risk Management
references.note: Treats an exposure as restructured where a borrower in financial difficulty is given a concession the bank would not otherwise grant.

programs.title: Australia | Loan Provisioning and Impairment (APS 220 and Accounting Standards)
programs.why: APS 220 requires banks to have credit risk practices and internal controls that consistently produce adequate provisions under their policies and Australian Accounting Standards (the expected credit loss model). Staff involved in provisioning need to understand this; no course is set.

references.title: APS 220 Credit Risk Management
references.note: Banks must determine adequate provisions consistently, following their own policies and Australian Accounting Standards, supported by effective internal control.

programs.title: Australia | Security Valuation and Collateral (APRA APS 220)
programs.why: APS 220 requires a security valuation policy that sets the qualifications and experience needed by internal valuers and robust selection of external valuers based on qualifications, experience and local knowledge. It sets competence criteria rather than a course.

references.title: APS 220 Credit Risk Management
references.note: Banks must set the qualifications and experience required of internal appraisers, choose external valuers on professional qualifications, relevant experience and insurance, and control the use of automated or alternative valuation methods.

programs.title: Australia | Credit Reporting Compliance (Privacy Act Part IIIA and CR Code 2025)
audience: Staff handling credit reporting or credit eligibility information
programs.why: The registered Privacy (Credit Reporting) Code 2025, which binds credit providers such as banks, requires them to take reasonable steps to tell employees who handle credit reporting or credit eligibility information about the Part IIIA rules and to train them in the procedures and systems that achieve compliance.

references.title: Privacy (Credit Reporting) Code 2025
references.issuer: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: Credit providers must take reasonable steps to inform employees who handle credit reporting or credit eligibility information of the relevant requirements and to train them in the practices, procedures and systems designed to meet them. Replaced the 2024 code on 25 March 2025.

references.title: Privacy Act 1988
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: Sets the rules on collecting, using, disclosing, correcting and securing credit reporting and credit eligibility information, for credit reporting bodies and credit providers.

programs.title: Australia | Consumer Credit under the NCCP Act and National Credit Code
programs.why: Credit licensees must keep their representatives adequately trained and competent for the credit activities they carry out (NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)), and the National Credit Code governs disclosure, hardship, enforcement and buy now pay later contracts. ASIC guidance in RG 206 expects initial and ongoing training.

references.title: National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: Licensees must maintain their own competence and ensure representatives are adequately trained and competent; the National Credit Code sets the rules for regulated consumer credit contracts, now including buy now pay later contracts.

programs.title: Australia | Unclaimed Money and Inactive Accounts (Banking Act s 69)
audience: Finance staff handling unclaimed money transfers
programs.why: Under the Banking Act, money in accounts with no customer deposit or withdrawal for seven years is treated as unclaimed and transferred to the Commonwealth through ASIC; fees and interest do not count as activity. Operations staff must apply these rules and help customers reclaim money; no course is prescribed.

references.title: Banking Act 1959
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: Sets the unclaimed moneys regime for ADI accounts, including transfer to the Commonwealth, disclosure of information and powers about deceased depositors' money.

references.title: Changes to the Commonwealth unclaimed money laws
references.note: Explains that since 31 December 2015 bank accounts become unclaimed after seven years without deposits or withdrawals; fees and interest are not activity and some account types are exempt.

programs.title: Australia | ePayments Code Compliance
programs.why: Most Australian banks subscribe to ASIC's ePayments Code, which binds them to rules on terms and statements, liability for unauthorised transactions, passcode security and recovering mistaken internet payments. It is a voluntary code with no training clause, so staff need working knowledge rather than a set course.

references.title: ePayments Code
references.note: Voluntary code administered by ASIC; sets rules for disclosure, unauthorised transaction liability, passcode security, mistaken internet payments and complaints for subscribers. Updated version published 2 June 2022 with compliance required by 2 June 2023.

references.title: ePayments Code
references.note: ASIC page stating that the code is currently voluntary, that most banks, credit unions and building societies subscribe, and that it only protects customers of subscribers.

programs.title: Australia | Psychosocial Hazards and Workplace Bullying (WHS)
programs.why: Under the model WHS laws employers must eliminate or minimise psychosocial risks, including bullying and harassment. Safe Work Australia guidance treats training and supervision as support for those controls.

references.title: Psychosocial hazards
references.note: Employers must eliminate or minimise psychosocial risks, including bullying and harassment, so far as reasonably practicable.

references.title: Model Code of Practice: Managing psychosocial hazards at work
references.note: Practical guidance on controls for psychosocial risks, supported by training and supervision.

programs.title: Australia | Sex Discrimination Act Positive Duty
programs.why: Employers must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate sexual harassment, and the Commission can enforce this from 12 December 2023. Its guidelines expect compulsory, ongoing training but the Act does not prescribe it.

references.title: Sex Discrimination Act 1984
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: Employers and PCBUs must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate, as far as possible, unlawful sex discrimination, sexual harassment, sex-based harassment, hostile workplace environments and related victimisation; training is not named in the Act.

references.title: Guidelines for Complying with the Positive Duty under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth)
references.note: Employers must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate sexual harassment; the Commission expects compulsory, ongoing, expert-led training, with more for leaders.

references.title: A Quick Guide for Complying with the Positive Duty under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984
references.note: Summarises the seven standards; training records and content are examples of compliance evidence. Enforcement powers from 12 December 2023.

programs.title: Australia | Work Health and Safety Duties
programs.why: The primary WHS duty requires employers to provide the information, training, instruction or supervision needed to protect workers from health and safety risks. State and territory laws apply this; Victoria has its own OHS Act.

references.title: Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Cth)
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: The primary duty of care includes ensuring, so far as reasonably practicable, the information, training, instruction or supervision needed to protect all persons from work health and safety risks. States and territories have mirror laws; Victoria has its own OHS Act.

references.title: Guide to the Work Health and Safety Act
references.provision: Model WHS Act s 19 (primary duty of care)
references.note: Explains the primary duty of care in the model WHS Act, which includes providing the information, training, instruction or supervision needed to protect workers.

programs.title: Australia | APRA Prudential Reporting (Reporting Standards)
programs.why: Banks must lodge APRA returns under reporting standards such as ARS 110.0 on capital adequacy, and CPS 220 requires risk data good enough for accurate, timely reporting. Reporting staff need to know the forms and instructions; no training is prescribed.

references.title: ARS 110.0 Capital Adequacy
references.note: Reporting standard and form for reporting capital adequacy to APRA, read with APS 110 and APS 111.

references.title: CPS 220 Risk Management
references.note: Requires management information and a robust data framework for timely and accurate measurement and reporting of material risks.

programs.title: Australia | Pillar 3 Public Disclosure (APRA APS 330)
programs.why: APS 330 requires significant banks to publish information on capital, liquidity and risk exposures, aligned with Basel disclosure requirements. Staff preparing disclosures need to know the rules; no course is set.

references.title: APS 330 Public Disclosure
references.note: Significant financial institution banks must publish prescribed information on capital, liquidity and risk exposures, with reference to the Basel Committee disclosure requirements.

programs.title: Australia | FATCA Due Diligence and Reporting (TAA 1953 Subdiv 396-A)
programs.why: Australian financial institutions must identify and report US accounts to the ATO under the Australia-US FATCA agreement. Staff who collect self-certifications or report need procedural knowledge; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Taxation Administration Act 1953
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Schedule 1, Subdivision 396-A (FATCA) and Subdivision 396-C (Common Reporting Standard)
references.note: Sets the FATCA and CRS due diligence and reporting duties of Australian financial institutions; it does not prescribe staff training.

references.title: Automatic exchange of information – CRS and FATCA: 1 Introduction
references.note: Explains that Australian financial institutions' CRS and FATCA duties arise under Subdivisions 396-C and 396-A of Schedule 1 to the Taxation Administration Act 1953.

references.title: Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act
references.note: ATO page on the Australia-US FATCA agreement and reporting by Australian financial institutions.

references.title: Self-review guide and toolkit
references.note: ATO toolkit to help financial institutions assess the effectiveness of their CRS and FATCA compliance frameworks.

programs.title: Australia | Common Reporting Standard (TAA 1953 Subdiv 396-C)
programs.why: Banks must apply CRS due diligence, including self-certifications, and report foreign tax resident accounts to the ATO, following the OECD Commentary. The ATO's toolkit helps test the framework.

references.title: Taxation Administration Act 1953
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Schedule 1, Subdivision 396-A (FATCA) and Subdivision 396-C (Common Reporting Standard)
references.note: Sets the FATCA and CRS due diligence and reporting duties of Australian financial institutions; it does not prescribe staff training.

references.title: Automatic exchange of information – CRS and FATCA: 1 Introduction
references.note: Explains that Australian financial institutions' CRS and FATCA duties arise under Subdivisions 396-C and 396-A of Schedule 1 to the Taxation Administration Act 1953.

references.title: Automatic exchange of information – CRS and FATCA: 4 Due diligence
references.note: Due diligence procedures for identifying reportable accounts, including self-certification checks for new accounts.

references.title: Self-review guide and toolkit
references.note: ATO toolkit to help financial institutions assess the effectiveness of their CRS and FATCA compliance frameworks.

programs.title: Australia | Insider Trading and Market Misconduct (Corporations Act Part 7.10)
audience: Staff with access to inside information
programs.why: Part 7.10 of the Corporations Act prohibits market manipulation, false trading and insider trading, and bank market participants must report suspected insider trading or manipulation to ASIC under the market integrity rules. Staff need to recognise and escalate these risks, but no course is prescribed.

references.title: Corporations Act 2001
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: Prohibits market manipulation and other market misconduct and bars dealing or procuring while in possession of inside information.

references.title: ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) 2017
references.note: A market participant with reasonable grounds to suspect insider trading or market manipulation must notify ASIC and keep the notification confidential.

programs.title: Australia | ASIC Market Integrity Rules for Market Participants
programs.why: Banks that are trading participants on ASX or other markets must ensure each designated trading representative is suitably qualified and experienced and has shown knowledge of the market's dealing rules before submitting orders, and that compliance is supervised by people with suitable skills and experience.

references.title: ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) 2017
references.note: Market participants need supervision by staff with appropriate skills, knowledge and experience; each DTR must be authorised, suitably qualified and experienced, and must demonstrate knowledge of the dealing rules before submitting trading messages. Latest compilation 15 October 2024.

programs.title: Australia | Consumer Data Right (Open Banking) Compliance
audience: Staff with access to CDR data in an accredited data recipient
Open banking product and technology teams
programs.why: Banks are data holders under the Consumer Data Right, and those accredited as data recipients must run a formal security training and awareness program: everyone interacting with CDR data must be trained in security and privacy before access, with refresher training at least once a year.

references.title: Competition and Consumer (Consumer Data Right) Rules 2020
references.provision: Schedule 2, Part 2, clause 2.2 (security training and awareness control)
references.note: Accredited data recipients must have a formal information security training and awareness program: security and privacy training before staff interact with the CDR data environment and refresher courses at least annually. Schedule 3 covers banking sector data holders.

notes: AML/CTF reform: the AML/CTF Amendment Act 2024 and the AML/CTF Rules 2025 (which replaced the 2007 Rules) applied to existing reporting entities such as banks from 31 March 2026; newly regulated professions followed on 1 July 2026. Personnel due diligence and training now sit in the AML/CTF policies (Act s 26F(4)(d) and (e); Rules ss 5-8 and 5-9), and the policies must also deal with targeted financial sanctions (Rules s 5-3).
AUSTRAC transition: existing reporting entities may keep using the old SMR form and content until 30 March 2029 (Rules s 12-2); the new tipping-off offence began 31 March 2025.
APRA CPS 230 took effect on 1 July 2025, replacing CPS 231 and CPS 232; targeted amendments for certain non-traditional service providers apply from 1 July 2026.
APRA consulted in mid-2026 on a revised CPS 510 that would absorb CPS 520 fit and proper requirements; check whether it has been finalised.

Scams Prevention Framework: banks must join AFCA for SPF purposes by 1 September 2026, and most obligations under the banking code start 31 March 2027; the code was still a draft when consulted on in 2026.

Privacy Act reforms (2024 amending Act): statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy, tiered penalties, automated decision transparency due December 2026, and a Children's Online Privacy Code due by 10 December 2026.
The 2025 Banking Code of Practice took effect on 28 February 2025 with broader vulnerability commitments.
A corporate offence of failing to prevent foreign bribery (Criminal Code s 70.5A) now applies, with an adequate procedures defence and Attorney-General's guidance.
APRA's CPS 230 page shows the guide CPG 230 as superseded on 30 June 2026; entries citing CPG 230 should be re-checked against the current guidance before relying on them.

APRA has refreshed many bank prudential standards: APS 110, APS 116 and APS 330 versions from 1 January 2025, APS 111, APS 112 and APS 210 from 1 July 2025, APS 117 from 1 October 2025 and APS 113 from 30 June 2026. The Privacy (Credit Reporting) Code 2025 replaced the 2024 code on 25 March 2025.
